Schwarz, Man Ray, The Rigour of Imagination, London, 1977, no. 90 (illustrated p. 91, without the dedication). | Exh. cat., Man Ray, 1890-1976, Ronny van de Velde, Antwerp, 1994, no. 493 (illustrated without the dedication). | | | The following works come from the estate of Hugo and Selma van de Perre, a couple whose lives and friendships were deeply entwined with twentieth-century European culture. United by intellectual curiosity and a shared commitment to art, literature and political thought, they assembled a collection shaped less by connoisseurship alone than by personal connection. Much of it derives from the estate of E. L. T. Mesens, the poet, artist and gallerist who played a decisive role in shaping Surrealism in Britain following the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London. | | Hugo van de Perre, the son of Alfons van de Perre, founder of the Belgian newspaper De Standaard, was a journalist, cultural commentator and close confidant of Mesens. Their friendship was both intellectual and deeply personal. When Mesens died in 1971, Hugo wrote his obituary — Elegie om E.L.T. Mesens — published in De Spectator (Brussels) in June of that year. In it, he described Mesens not merely as a Surrealist organiser or polemicist, but as a fiercely independent spirit, defined by loyalty, moral conviction and a belief in art as a lived position rather than a profession. The text reveals a friendship founded on shared values: resistance to conformity, devotion to artistic freedom, and an unwavering commitment to the ethical force of culture. It was Hugo, as executor of Mesens' estate, who ensured that many of these works were preserved within a private collection shaped by memory and trust. | | Selma van de Perre was a Dutch–British freedom fighter and member of the wartime resistance, later settling in London where she studied anthropology and sociology and worked at the BBC. She and Hugo married in 1955 and remained deeply engaged with cultural life in Britain and on the Continent. After Hugo's death in 1979, Selma continued his work as a foreign correspondent for Belgian broadcasters and newspapers, reporting particularly on British art and music. The collection they formed together reflects this outward-looking sensibility: international in scope, human in scale, and attentive to the emotional charge of works made and exchanged among friends. | | A jewel of the present group is Man Ray's Rêve du 25 nov 1936, a drawing of exceptional intimacy and historical resonance. Executed in 1936 as an illustration for Les Mains libres, Man Ray's celebrated collaboration with Paul Éluard, the present sheet is uniquely inscribed and dedicated by the artist to Mesens — 'pour Édouard son ami'. The work's early exhibition history underscores its importance within the international dissemination of Surrealism: shown at major early Man Ray exhibitions at the Valentine Gallery in New York in 1936, at Galerie Jeanne Bucher in Paris in 1937 — one of the leading avant-garde galleries of the period — and later at the The London Gallery in 1939, the epicentre of British Surrealism under Mesens' direction. | | Man Ray often explained that many drawings for Les Mains libres were made immediately upon waking, translated directly from dreams before rational interpretation could intervene. The present work belongs to a moment of intense retrospection. In November 1936, Man Ray was in New York for the landmark exhibition Fantastic Art, Dada, Surrealism at the Museum of Modern Art — a symbolic homecoming after fifteen years in Paris. From his hotel terrace overlooking Central Park, he photographed the city, later cropping out a synagogue that had anchored the original image — a quiet but telling gesture reflecting his complex relationship to Jewish identity, which he had long masked through name changes and self-reinvention. The composition of that photograph is directly evoked in the present work, which evokes the impressive verticality of Fifth Avenue's high rise buildings, intersected by the environs of Central Park. The drawing's airborne locomotive evokes not only Man Ray's childhood memories and early fascinations with machines, but also the notorious 1895 train crash at the Gare Montparnasse in Paris, an image widely circulated in illustrated newspapers and lodged in the modern imagination. Within Surrealism, trains recur as potent symbols — such as in the works of Belgian Surrealist Paul Delvaux — embodying passage between realms, between dreams and waking life, reality and fantasy. Here, the train becomes an agent of psychic transit, a vehicle of unconscious return. | | That this drawing passed directly from Man Ray to Mesens, and from Mesens' estate into the collection of Hugo and Selma van de Perre, is profoundly significant. It encapsulates Surrealism not merely as an aesthetic movement, but as a network of lived relationships, sustained by generosity, loyalty and shared belief in art's capacity to bridge inner and outer worlds. Seen alongside works by Méret Oppenheim, António Pedro and Mesens himself, the present work anchors the collection as a testament to Surrealism's human core — an art of friendship, exchange and imaginative freedom, preserved here with remarkable integrity.

Lemoisne, Degas et son oeuvre, Vol. III, Paris, 1947, no. 1179 (illustrated p. 685); and sold: the artist's estate; their sale, Galerie Georges Petit, Sale III, Paris, 9 April 1919, lot 74). Degas held the work in particular esteem, using his experimental counterproof process to transfer and reverse the onto a second sheet. To produce such works, Degas placed a new sheet over the original pastel and introduced controlled moisture before applying pressure, allowing the image to transfer in reverse. This process not only sharpened compositional relationships but also introduced subtle tonal variations and surface effects inherent to the technique. Degas frequently treated these counterproofs as autonomous works, reworking them further in pastel or charcoal, and valuing them as opportunities for refinement of his compositions. Although the technique had largely fallen out of use by the nineteenth century, it appealed to Degas for the productive tension it created between chance and control. Such works occupy a distinctive place within his practice, reflecting both technical experimentation and aesthetic refinement. | | The present work was formerly in the collection of Julie Manet, daughter of Berthe Morisot and Édouard Manet. Together with her husband, Ernest Rouart – whom Degas mentored in painting and drawing – she assembled one of the most distinguished private collections of Impressionist art in France, including important works by Manet, Morisot, Degas, Monet, Renoir and Pissarro. The Rouart family occupied a central position within the Impressionist circle: Henri Rouart, Ernest's father, was both a painter and one of the earliest and most important patrons of Degas and his contemporaries, forming a collection that later entered museums worldwide. Degas played an active role in encouraging the relationship between Ernest Rouart and Julie Manet, both of whom he knew intimately, and whose union further strengthened the close personal and artistic bonds between the Manet, Morisot, and Rouart families. The present work thus embodies both Degas's relentless technical experimentation and its intimate passage through one of the most significant lineages of Impressionist art.

Strobl, Gustav Klimt, Vol. III, Die Zeichnungen, 1912-1918, Salzburg, 1984, no. 2781 (illustrated p. 167). | | | Before his death in 1918, Gustave Klimt focused extensively on figure studies in pencil, exploring the autonomous expressive potential of line. Stehender Akt nach rechts is a compelling example from this mature period. Devoting particular attention to the standing female nude, Klimt rendered these subjects with remarkable economy of means, moving away from the decorative density of his celebrated paintings. | | In the present work, the model stands oriented to the right, her body articulated through a refined, continuous contour. The figure's weight settles subtly into one hip, forming a gentle contrapposto that recalls the classical canon. Yet the treatment diverges fundamentally from nineteenth-century academic life study: rather than constructing the body through chiaroscuro and anatomical modelling, Klimt privileges line as the primary vehicle of form. Limbs and torso are defined by contour alone, and the volumes of the body emerge with deceptive simplicity. | | Detached from mythological or allegorical narrative and presented without contextual framing, the model exists in a space that is neither constructed nor described. The blank expanse of paper surrounding the figure thereby reinforces the autonomy of line. In contrast to academic tradition, which sought to stabilise the body within a codified system of proportion and moral decorum, Klimt approaches the female figure as a living, mutable presence. | | The model's head, delicately articulated, introduces a psychological dimension that distinguishes the work. Although minimally described, the facial features anchor the figure's corporeality and suggest an individual presence rather than an abstract type. In this respect, Klimt revisits the long tradition of the academic standing nude only to reconfigure it: the body is neither heroic nor didactic, but intimate, contemporary and profoundly human. | | Executed in the final years of his life, Stehender Akt nach rechts reflects an artist who, having traversed the realms of Symbolism, Secessionist decoration, and painterly opulence, returned to drawing as a site for concentrated inquiry. In its restraint and clarity, the sheet stands as a testament to Klimt's profound redefinition of the nude — no longer a vehicle of academic virtuosity, but a locus of modern subjectivity and the enduring primacy of line.

These years coincide with the artist's early maturity within the Vienna Secession, a period during which his studies of the nude became increasingly autonomous, exploratory, and psychologically resonant. | | The model is shown seated and viewed from the front, her body folded inward upon itself. Her bowed head and curved spine establish a rhythmic, sinuous movement, articulated through a sequence of soft, looping contours that travel across the figure like a slow breath. Rather than constructing the body through tonal modelling or anatomical exactitude, Klimt allows form to emerge almost entirely from the delicacy of the pencil line. The figure seems less built than revealed. | | Such an approach marks a profound departure from the nineteenth-century academic life study, in which the seated nude functioned primarily as an exercise in proportion, structure, and ideal form. Here, Klimt abandons the stabilising conventions of spatial setting, directional light, and volumetric shading. The body floats outside measurable space, freed from the weight of environment and narrative. | | At this moment, Klimt was deeply engaged with the expressive and symbolic potential of the female body. The lowered head, obscuring the face, shifts attention away from individual likeness toward a state of inwardness. Identity dissolves into posture, as psychology is conveyed through curvature and restraint. In Sitzender Frauenakt von vorne, line becomes a sensitive instrument of perception, tracing not only the contour of the body but the atmosphere of introspection that surrounds it. The drawing thus participates in a broader transformation: the female nude is no longer presented as an academic exemplar or allegorical type, but as a locus of modern subjectivity. | | Sitzender Frauenakt von vorne therefore exemplifies Klimt's early mastery of linear expression, laying the groundwork for the increasingly fluid and experimental figure studies of the following decade. It stands as a testament to his investigation into the expressive capacity of contour, at a moment when modern art was rethinking the human form.

provenance: Private collection, UK (acquired directly from the artist in the 1960s). | Private collection, UK (by descent from the above). | | | Born into a Romanian Jewish Hasidic family, Reuven Rubin was a pioneer of Israeli art, instrumental in shaping a distinctive modern painterly language associated with Eretz Yisrael. Having spent his formative years in Romania, France, the United States and Palestine, Rubin developed a deliberately naïve style informed by his travels and by European modernism. This synthesis found expression in bold colour, simplified form and a childlike sense of wonder that permeates his oeuvre. In The flute player, this so-called 'primitive' manner is especially evident in the vibrant greens, reds and purples that animate the composition with rhythmic intensity. | | The painting draws on a key Hasidic tale centred on a simple shepherd boy who cannot read or pray, yet longs to participate in the Yom Kippur service of the Baal Shem Tov, the Jewish mystic regarded as the founder of Hasidic Judaism. Unable to express himself through words, the boy plays a single, heartfelt note on his flute. This pure and unmediated act of devotion was said to affirm that sincere longing and spiritual intensity surpass formal knowledge and learned ritual. In Hasidic teachings, the flute player thus became a potent symbol of raw faith, serving as a bridge between the earthly and the divine. | | The present work may therefore be understood as emblematic of a broader moment in which Jewish artists sought new visual languages through which to articulate cultural, spiritual and national identity. For Rubin in particular, the flute-playing shepherd came to embody a renewed Hebrew spirit — at once ancient and modern — in which faith, landscape and the ideals of national revival converge in a single, resonant image. | | The owners of the present work look fondly upon their memories of meeting Rubin and his wife Esther in Tel Aviv, visiting the artist in his studio and engaging directly with his painted world. It was in this intimate setting that they encountered and acquired The flute player. Having remained in the same private collection since its acquisition, the work retains a direct and personal link to the artist himself, standing not only as a poetic expression of Rubin's vision, but also as a testament to the lived relationships that shaped and sustained his artistic life.

provenance: Kurimanzutto, Mexico City | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | Exhibited | Mexico City, Anahuacalli Diego Rivera Museum, Nuds, 21 April - 8 July 2012 (in collaboration with Kurimanzutto, Mexico City) | | | | Executed in 2012, Maradona belongs to a significant body of sculptural work in which Sarah Lucas reconfigures the human figure through a vocabulary of provisional materials and abject humour. Emerging from the context of the Young British Artists in the early 1990s, Lucas has consistently challenged art historical conventions surrounding the nude, gender representation and sculptural monumentality. In Maradona, these concerns are distilled into a work that is at once formally spare and conceptually layered. | | The sculpture is constructed from aluminium wire framework wrapped with tape and padded with cotton, over which taut Lycra stockings are stretched to create a sagging, flesh-like surface. The figure is anchored and partially elevated by stone bricks, whose weight and rectilinear geometry contrast sharply with the soft, knotted materiality above. Lucas's materials are deliberately unheroic: industrial wire, hosiery and building blocks replace marble or bronze, subverting the grand tradition of figurative sculpture. The resulting form appears at once skeletal and bodily; its limbs contorted into a configuration that resists stable anatomical reading. As in many of Lucas's works, the body is suggested rather than described; it is fragmented, doubled back upon itself, and ambiguously gendered. | | The title Maradona invokes the legendary Argentine footballer Diego Maradona, a figure synonymous with virtuosity, charisma and scandal. This reference introduces a charged interplay between cultural mythology and physicality. Maradona's athletic prowess, particularly his balance, agility and controversial "Hand of God" goal, resonates ironically with the sculpture's precarious equilibrium and improvised construction. Lucas does not offer portraiture; instead, she mobilises the name as a cultural signifier, collapsing distinctions between high art and popular culture. The monumental expectations associated with a sporting icon are undercut by the work's awkward, anti-classical stance. | | Formally, the sculpture engages with the legacy of the reclining nude, a genre historically bound to ideals of beauty, passivity and erotic display. Lucas destabilises this lineage. The figure in Maradona neither reclines gracefully nor asserts heroic dominance; it slumps, twists and resists visual mastery. The stretched stockings evoke skin, yet their translucency exposes the armature beneath, denying illusionism and foregrounding construction. This oscillation between surface and structure mirrors Lucas's broader interrogation of how bodies are culturally constructed and consumed. | | The bricks function both structurally and symbolically. Their earth-bound solidity contrasts with the elastic tension of the hosiery, introducing a dialogue between weight and lightness, permanence and improvisation. They also suggest the language of minimalism, recalling the industrial units of 1960s sculpture, yet here they serve not as autonomous forms but as supports for an unruly, quasi-figurative mass. Lucas thus stages a confrontation between modernist formalism and corporeal excess. | | The present work was exhibited in the artist's solo exhibition at the Anahuacalli Diego Rivera Museum in 2012, where it was situated among sculptures and installations that further examined themes of embodiment, materiality and cultural symbolism. Within this context, Maradona formed part of a broader exploration of how the body - athletic, sexualised, celebrated or abject - is constructed and reconfigured through both physical matter and linguistic designation. | | At once irreverent and exacting, Maradona distils the central tensions that define Sarah Lucas's sculptural practice. Monumental in implication yet provisional in execution, the work refuses the stability and authority historically granted to the figure, proposing instead a body that is elastic, contingent and perpetually renegotiated, shaped as much by cultural projection as by physical structure. In its precarious calibration of weight and levity, humour and critique, the sculpture encapsulates the clarity of vision and material intelligence that have secured Lucas's position among the most influential artists of her generation. Over more than three decades, the artist has remained unwavering in her commitment to challenging the hierarchies of both form and subject matter, expanding the possibilities of sculpture through unorthodox materials and a distinctly incisive wit. Maradona not only stands as a pointed meditation on how icons are constructed and undone, but also as a compelling testament to the artist's sustained and consequential contribution to the development of contemporary sculpture in the twenty-first century.

provenance: Private Collection, Barcelona | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | Exhibited | Bruges, Garden of the Groeninge Museum, A Journey Between Matter and Light, Pablo Atchugarry, 24 June - 31 October 2006 (illustrated p. 236) | | Literature | Exh. cat., Pablo Atchugarry, Le infinite evoluzioni del marmo, Lecco, 2001 (illustrated p. 117) | Carlo Pirovano, Atchugarry, Catalogo generale della scultura, Vol. I, Milan, 2013, no. 43 (illustrated p. 331) | | | | Rising with serene authority, Pareja Estelar by Pablo Atchugarry unfolds as a poised and meditative exploration of vertical form, its elegant silhouette commanding attention and inviting contemplation. Carved from pink Portugal marble, animated by darker veins of red and orange, the work bears visible traces of geological time. These natural markings traverse the polished surface like organic currents, underscoring the dynamic interplay between material permanence and sculptural refinement. Under Atchugarry's hand, the marble is neither passive nor resistant; it is transformed into a resonant medium for light, movement, and spiritual suggestion. Extending to over two meters high, the sculpture asserts a commanding presence while retaining a sense of ethereal lightness. | | A committed practitioner of direct carving, Atchugarry approaches marble with sustained attention to it's essential plastic qualities, surface modulation, texture, spatial articulation, and the orchestration of light. Despite its considerable mass, the sculpture conveys an impression of levity. Its attenuated, ascending contours seems to counteract gravity, creating a visual tension between weight and lift. The pronounced verticality establishes a compositional logic of ascent: elongated pleats rise in rhythmic succession, gathering and releasing in a sequence of shadowed recesses and illuminated ridges. As the viewer moves around the work, the nearly symmetrical folds generate subtle variations in light and depth, producing a form that appears animated and responsive. At its centre, a restrained opening introduces a measured void, a spatial pause that invites contemplation and suggests both interiority and latent potential. | | Atchugarry's aesthetic language situates his practice within a distinguished sculptural lineage. His reverence for marble recalls the disciplined material engagement of Michelangelo and the refined neoclassicism of Antonia Canova, while his sensitivity to abstraction and void resonates with the formal investigations of Henry Moore and Isamu Noguchi. Parallels may also be drawn with Constantin Brancusi, particularly in the pursuit of essential form and transcendence through reduction. Yet Atchugarry's sculptural voice remains distinctly his own. His sustained commitment to hand-carving, coupled with a humanistic sensitivity to rhythm and proportion, imbues each work with a sense of intimacy and deliberation. The recurring upward thrust that characterises much of his oeuvre operates not merely as a formal device but as an expressive gesture – an articulation of aspiration and continuity. | | The warm tonality of the pink marble tempers the austerity often associated with stone, introducing subtle chromatic softness that enhances the sculpture's emotive presence. Light glides across its polished planes and gathers in its recesses, activating the surrounding space and reinforcing the work's dialogic relationship with its environment. | | Ultimately the present work may be understood as both material and metaphysical: firmly grounded in the substance of marble yet orientated towards transcendence. It stands as a compelling demonstration of Atchugarry's technical mastery and conceptual clarity, offering collectors a work that unites historical awareness, formal sophistication, and contemplative resonance.

provenance: Vrej Baghoomian Gallery, New York | Anon. sale, Sotheby's, New York, 29 September 1994, lot 486 | Private Collection, Spain | Acquired from the above by the present owner | | | | Painted in 1983, the present work belongs to a decisive formative moment in George Condo's oeuvre, a period in which the artist first consolidated the pictorial language that would define his career. Executed only a few years after his arrival in New York and at the dawn of his mature practice, this canvas demonstrates Condo's early synthesis of painterly tradition, cartoon distortion, and psychological fragmentation, an approach he would later describe as "Artificial Realism." | | Set against a dark, atmospheric ground animated by calligraphic red and white arabesques, the composition is dominated by a suspended, mask-like head that appears to hover in indeterminate space. The figure is neither fully human nor entirely abstract; rather, it is an amalgamation of anatomical fragments, vegetal forms, and painterly invention. A central white, bone-like structure bisects the face vertically, suggesting both skeletal armature and heraldic device. Around it cluster bulbous, jewel-toned forms, grapes, fleshy protrusions, and ocular motifs, that destabilise any singular reading of the image. The work oscillates between still life, portrait, and grotesque spirit. | | This hybridity is characteristic of Condo's early 1980s production; while contemporaneous with the resurgence of figurative painting in New York, his work diverged from the raw immediacy of Neo-Expressionism by engaging more self-consciously with art history. Even at this early stage, Condo's figures evoke the compositional gravity and chiaroscuro of Old Master painting, filtered through a lens of distortion indebted to modernism. The present work reveals an artist testing the elasticity of representation: features are exaggerated, displaced, or multiplied, yet remain coherently structured within a classical vertical format. | | The black ground, energised by looping linear gestures, further situates the painting within the experimental climate of the early 1980s. These marks function simultaneously as spatial framework and expressive residue, enclosing the central head while allowing it to vibrate against the void. The tension between containment and dissolution, between classical order and grotesque excess, would become a defining dialectic throughout Condo's career. | | Most importantly, 1983 marks a period in which Condo began to move beyond straightforward caricature toward a more complex psychological construction of the figure. The fragmentation seen here anticipates the multi-perspectival faces that would later culminate in his concept of "Psychological Cubism." In this early work, however, the fractures are more visceral than analytical; the image feels grown rather than constructed, organic rather than architectural. The thick, confident brushwork and saturated palette convey a young artist asserting both technical command and conceptual ambition. | | Untitled stands at a critical juncture in the artist's trajectory; it is neither tentative nor derivative, but rather it evidences the moment in which Condo's distinctive visual language crystallised. The present work captures Condo's emergence as a leading figure in postwar figurative painting. The suspended, fractured head balances classical compositional rigor with expressive invention, revealing a painter already redefining representation through psychological and formal complexity. This work crystallises the ambitions of Condo's early years, positioning the artist at the forefront of a generation reshaping portraiture and stands as a compelling testament to the originality and enduring impact of his formative breakthrough.
